p1.key: C(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g) → 2CO(g) goes from one mole of gas to two moles of gas, the largest increase in disorder. B and C decrease or keep the number of gas moles; A forms aqueous ions only.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −597.3 − 300(−0.33) = −498 kJ, so it is spontaneous at 300 K. Since ΔS is negative, −TΔS grows more positive as T rises, and ΔG becomes positive above T = 597.3/0.33 ≈ 1800 K.
Decomposing water is the reverse of the strongly exothermic combustion of hydrogen, so it is endothermic. It goes from 2 mol to 3 mol of gas, so entropy increases significantly.
H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) → 2HI(g) has 2 mol gas on each side, so ΔS ≈ 0. A and D reduce the moles of gas (ΔS negative), and B forms a gas from a liquid (ΔS positive).
Decomposing a solid ionic compound into two gases needs energy (ΔH +). Going from a solid to 2 mol of gas greatly increases disorder (ΔS +).
Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO<sub>2</sub>(g) has 3 mol gas on each side, so ΔS ≈ 0. A loses gas moles, C turns a gas into aqueous ions, and D produces gas.
Sodium corroding in air (4Na(s) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 2Na<sub>2</sub>O(s)) uses up gas to form a solid, so entropy decreases. Sublimation, dissolving and mixing of gases all increase disorder.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH negative and ΔS negative, ΔG is negative at low T, but the −TΔS term becomes more positive as T rises, eventually making ΔG positive (non-spontaneous).
In H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) → 2HI(g) there are 2 mol of gas on each side, so ΔS is close to zero. Each other reaction changes the amount of gas.
A negative ΔG means the reaction is thermodynamically spontaneous (feasible). ΔG says nothing about rate, and a reaction with ΔG < 0 can be endothermic if ΔS is large enough.
Combustion is exothermic (ΔH −). Gas moles increase from 27 to 34, so ΔS is +. With ΔH − and ΔS +, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative at all temperatures.
Count gas moles: A 2.5 → 3 (Δn = +0.5); B 2.5 → 1; C 3 → 3; D 3 → 1. Only A increases the amount of gas, so it has the greatest positive ΔS.

p1.key: Entropy increases most when the number of moles of gas increases. Only B makes gas (CO<sub>2</sub>) from a solid; C decreases gas moles, D keeps them the same, and A is solids only.
T = 27 + 273 = 300 K. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −10 000 J − (300 K × −10 J K−1) = −10 000 + 3000 = −7000 J. Remember to convert kJ to J.

Cooling reduces the kinetic energy of the molecules, so fewer energy arrangements are available and entropy falls. Adding more gas increases entropy, and sunlight splits Cl<sub>2</sub> into radicals, increasing particle number.
With ΔH and ΔS both positive, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS depends on T: it is positive at low temperature and becomes negative at high temperature. So C is wrong, and the reverse reaction is exothermic.
Entropy rises most when the moles of gas increase. C goes from 2 to 4 mol gas. A (4 → 2) and D (3 → 2) decrease gas moles, and B involves only solids.
In A, 3 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas, so disorder decreases and ΔS is negative. B (solid → gas) and D (more gas molecules) increase entropy; in C the gas moles are unchanged (2 → 2).
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH and ΔS both negative, −TΔS is positive and grows with T, so ΔG becomes less negative: the reaction becomes less spontaneous as temperature rises (spontaneous only at low T).
Condensation (gas → liquid) reduces the freedom and disorder of the particles, so entropy decreases. Mixing gases, heating a liquid and dissolving a solid all increase entropy.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. If ΔH is negative and ΔS positive, both terms make ΔG negative at every temperature, so the reaction is always spontaneous.
ΔG° = ΣΔGf°(products) − ΣΔGf°(reactants) = −834 − (−570 + −237) = −834 + 807 = −27 kJ mol⁻¹. Negative ΔG°, so the reaction is spontaneous.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH positive and ΔS negative, −TΔS is also positive, so ΔG is positive at every temperature: the reaction is never spontaneous.

Dissolving solid NaCl spreads ordered lattice ions through the solution, so entropy increases. A, B and C all go from a more disordered to a more ordered state (gas → solid/liquid, liquid → solid). D.
In A, 3 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas, so the number of gas particles falls: ΔS is negative. B and D increase or keep the number of gas moles, and C (dissolving) increases entropy. A.

Only C produces a gas from no gaseous reactants (CO2 is released), giving the largest increase in entropy. A has 2 mol of gas on both sides, B shows little change, and D forms a solid precipitate (decrease). C.
The mixture heats up, so ΔH is negative. Two moles of liquid produce gas, so ΔS is positive. With ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is always negative.
Look at the change in moles of gas: C goes from 0 to 1 mol of gas (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>), the only large increase. A and B decrease the gas moles; D has no change (2 → 2).
Going from 4 mol to 2 mol of gas reduces the number of ways of arranging the particles, so entropy decreases. Heating, boiling and mixing all increase entropy.
With ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, both terms in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS are negative, so ΔG < 0 at every temperature.

Raising the temperature increases particle motion and shifts this endothermic decomposition to the right, producing more gas. Removing CO<sub>2</sub> also shifts the equilibrium right, forming more gas. Increasing pressure (adding CO<sub>2</sub>) shifts it left, reducing the gas.
Unlike ΔHf, standard entropies of elements are not zero, so I is false. ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants) = 2S°(NO2) − 2S°(NO) − S°(O2), and 3 mol gas → 2 mol gas gives ΔS° < 0.
For ΔG = ΔH − TΔS to become negative only at high T, ΔH and ΔS must both be positive. CaCO3 decomposition is endothermic and produces gas (ΔS > 0). D has ΔS < 0, so it is never spontaneous.
In C, 2 mol of gas form 1 mol of gas, so disorder and entropy decrease. A and B produce gas from non-gaseous reactants, and melting ice (D) increases entropy.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH and ΔS both positive, raising T makes the −TΔS term larger, so ΔG becomes more negative. The reaction becomes spontaneous above 179 000 / 161.0 ≈ 1110 K.
In A, 3 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas, so the system becomes more ordered and ΔS is negative. B makes gaseous ions from a solid (ΔS positive), and C and D keep the number of gas moles the same.
The temperature drops, so dissolving is endothermic (ΔH +). The process is spontaneous, so ΔG is negative. That is only possible if −TΔS outweighs ΔH, so ΔS must be positive.

I: the ions in a solid lattice become dispersed in solution, so entropy increases. II: a gas is produced, so entropy increases. III: aqueous ions combine to form a solid precipitate, so entropy decreases.
II: 9 mol of gas become 10 mol of gas, so entropy increases. III: liquid → gas, so entropy increases. I: gas → solid, a large decrease in entropy.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. If ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, both terms are negative, so ΔG < 0 at every temperature.

C produces 1 mol of gas from no gaseous reactants (solid + aqueous), so it has the largest entropy increase. A goes from 3 mol gas to 2 mol gas, while B and D also reduce the number of gas moles, so their ΔS is negative.
A reaction is spontaneous when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative. ΔH and ΔS can each have either sign for a spontaneous change.
I: liquid → solid, less disorder, ΔS negative. III: 3 mol gas → 2 mol gas, ΔS negative. II produces a gas from a liquid, so ΔS is positive. Answer: I and III only.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with ΔH positive and ΔS positive. At low T the TΔS term is small, so ΔG is positive; only at very high T (above 181000/25 ≈ 7240 K) does ΔG become negative.

Entropy increases solid < liquid < gas. Na(s) is lowest. Liquid Hg (a monatomic metal) has lower entropy than the more complex molecular liquid CH3OH, and gaseous propane is highest: Na(s) < Hg(l) < CH3OH(l) < C3H8(g).
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. If ΔH is positive and ΔS is negative, then −TΔS is also positive, so ΔG is positive at every temperature and the reaction is never spontaneous.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (ΔS in kJ). I: −100 − 300(−0.100) = −70 kJ, spontaneous. II: +100 + 30 = +130 kJ, not spontaneous. III: +100 − 3000(0.100) = −200 kJ, spontaneous. Answer: I and III only.
Entropy is lowest when particles are most ordered and have the least energy: a solid at low temperature. A gas at high temperature has the highest entropy.
Condensation makes the system more ordered, so ΔSsystem is negative. It is exothermic, and the heat released increases the entropy of the surroundings, so ΔSsurroundings is positive.
At equilibrium the system has reached the minimum Gibbs energy (ΔG = 0, no further spontaneous change). An isolated system changes spontaneously until its entropy is a maximum.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH positive and ΔS negative, both terms make ΔG positive at every temperature, so the reaction is never spontaneous.

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is a straight line with gradient −ΔS and intercept ΔH. The gradient is negative (ΔG falls as T rises), so ΔS is positive; extrapolating to T = 0 gives ΔH ≈ +59 kJ, i.e. ΔH is positive. The reaction becomes more spontaneous at higher T.
Combustion is exothermic (ΔH negative) and 6 mol gas becomes 12 mol gas (ΔS positive). ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is then negative at all temperatures: spontaneous.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. If ΔS < 0, the −TΔS term is positive and grows with T, so the reaction can be spontaneous only if ΔH is negative and T is low enough. A and B ignore the TΔS term.

In N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, 4 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas, a large drop in disorder, so ΔS is most negative. B and D produce gas (ΔS positive), and C has 3 aqueous particles on each side, so its change is small.

Spontaneous at low T but not at high T means ΔG = ΔH − TΔS goes from negative to positive as T rises. That needs ΔH negative and ΔS negative: −TΔS is positive and grows with T. This fits 1 mol of gas becoming a solid.
A system reaches equilibrium when its Gibbs energy is at a minimum (ΔG = 0, no further driving force). Taking system and surroundings together, the total entropy is at a maximum at equilibrium.
Condensation releases heat, so the enthalpy decreases (exothermic). Liquid particles are more ordered than gas particles, so the entropy decreases.
A positive ΔG° means the forward reaction is non-spontaneous and K < 1, so at equilibrium reactants are favoured. At equilibrium ΔG = 0; that is not the same as ΔG°.
Going from solid to gas (sublimation) gives the largest increase in disorder, so CO2(s) → CO2(g) has the greatest ΔS. B, C and D all form more ordered states (ΔS negative).
In B one solid forms 5 mol of gas (1 N2 + 4 H2O), the largest increase in moles of gas and so the largest ΔS. C forms only 1 mol of gas, and A and D form solids from gases (ΔS negative).
At equilibrium the Gibbs energy of the system is at a minimum (ΔG = 0), and the total entropy of system plus surroundings is at a maximum.
Two moles of gas become one mole of solid, a large decrease in disorder, so ΔS is most negative. Freezing water (C) is negative but smaller; A and B produce gas (ΔS positive).
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. If ΔH and ΔS are both positive, ΔG is positive at low T but becomes negative when TΔS > ΔH, i.e. at high temperature.
Heat released by the system goes to the surroundings, so ΔS<sub>surroundings</sub> = −ΔH/T. ΔH is therefore an indirect measure of the entropy change of the surroundings.

½Cl<sub>2</sub>(g) → Cl(g) increases the number of gas particles, and Li(s) → Li(g) turns a solid into a gas: both increase entropy. B's second change (gas ions → solid) and C's first change (atoms → molecules) decrease entropy.
ΔH − TΔS = ΔG. When ΔG = 0 there is no driving force in either direction: the system is at equilibrium. Reactions still occur, but at equal rates.
